title: Quality Assurance, AI and Automation Testing

blocks.text: 1. Software planning, development, testing, release, and improvement
2. IT foundations and early quality assurance
3. Manual testing and programming
4. Web automation, APIs, and continuous integration
5. Responsible AI use
6. A testing project on the existing website
7. Review requirements and acceptance criteria early
8. Identify ambiguity and risk before implementation
9. Continue testing through development, release, and maintenance
a. One website throughout the course
1. Use the existing website throughout the course
2. Add or refine forms, tables, asynchronous messages, and API-driven results
3. Use each addition for manual testing, automation, and regression
4. No new website build is required
a. What a learner can demonstrate at the end
1. Translate a feature request into acceptance criteria, risks, test scenarios, and traceable test cases.
2. Execute tests, investigate failures, document reproducible defects, and communicate release readiness.
3. Write browser tests with Selenium, Playwright, and Cypress, using reusable components and meaningful assertions.
4. Test APIs with Karate, run suites through Jenkins, and explain Docker, Kubernetes, AWS, and ServiceNow delivery workflows.
5. Explain LLMs and use Copilot to assist testing while checking outputs, limitations, and organizational data rules.
6. Present improvements to the existing website with a tested feature, regression evidence, and a clear handover.
7. Audience: beginners and career changers entering software quality assurance, plus manual testers moving into automation.
8. Delivery pace and assessment thresholds in this document are proposed settings for the course, not a fixed institutional or certification requirement.
b. Basis for this curriculum
1. This document draws on the Mini Quiz Tech & AI Academy hub scope, the revised integration plan, the SDLC Overview worked lesson, and the existing website project.
2. The detailed module sequence, suggested duration, grading, and project minimums are curriculum recommendations added to make that scope teachable from beginning to end.

sections.title: 5. How learning works in Mini Quiz Tech & AI Academy

blocks.text: a. A repeatable lesson cycle
1. Each lesson connects a short explanation to an observable action on the website.
2. Recall: Retrieve prior knowledge
3. Worked example: Study a demonstrated solution
4. Practice: Complete a focused exercise
5. Explanation: Describe the result and reasoning
6. Review: Revisit gaps in understanding
7. Mini quizzes support practice throughout the course; they do not replace practical assessment.
b. Notes and study guide
How we use it
1. Objectives: State what learners should understand or demonstrate
2. Plain-language explanations: Explain each concept in accessible terms
3. Website examples: Show how the concept applies to the existing website
4. Lesson sources: Record the references supporting the material
c. Mini quizzes
How we use it
1. Use short retrieval checks during class and a 25-question topic review.
2. Answer explanations: Describe why an answer is correct
3. Topic tags: Connect each question to its subject
4. Question identifiers: Give each question a stable reference
d. Flashcards
How we use it
1. Severity versus priority: Distinguish impact from urgency
2. Verification versus validation: Distinguish specified requirements from user needs
3. Waits versus retries: Distinguish readiness checks from repeated attempts
a. Carousels
How we use it
1. Present a visual sequence or comparison, usually 8 to 12 slides.
b. Hands on exercises
How we use it
1. Task: State the exercise to complete
2. Starter material: Supply the resources needed to begin
3. Expected evidence: Define what learners must submit
4. Self-check rubric: Help learners assess their own work
5. Learners execute and explain, not only watch.
c. Review and feedback
How we use it
1. Incorrect answers: Explain the reasoning error
2. Failed tests: Investigate the cause
3. Misconceptions: Correct the underlying misunderstanding
4. Spaced practice: Revisit earlier topics over time
a. A suggested guided session
1. Retrieval practice: 10 minutes
2. Teaching and demonstration: 20 minutes
3. Guided lab: 35 minutes
4. Independent variation: 15 minutes
5. Review: 10 minutes
6. Continue longer labs in the next class
7. Explain the reasoning before introducing more tools
b. The first worked lesson
1. The first SDLC lesson follows a small existing feature, such as recent scores, through planning, requirements, design, development, testing, deployment, and maintenance.
2. Requirement: Describe the selected feature on one page
3. Design sketch: Show how the feature will work
4. Test-plan outline: Define the testing approach
5. Release checklist: Identify checks required before release
6. Notes: Explain the lesson concepts
7. Quiz: Review the topic with 25 questions
8. Flashcards: Practice 25 key recall items
9. Carousel: Present the lesson visually
10. Lab: Apply the concepts hands on
11. Worksheet: Record the learner's work
12. The sample is a teaching draft.
13. Review its explanations before classroom use, especially simplified claims about development models and team responsibilities.
14. The instructor adapts it to the class and records corrections.
c. Before the first class
1. Check basic computer skills, file navigation, browser use, and reading of simple instructions.
2. Provide a browser, IDE, JDK, Node.js and npm, Git, build tools, and course repository access as each module needs them.
3. Provide an instructor-approved test environment with synthetic accounts and resettable data.
4. Use local fixtures or mocks when a service is unavailable.
Quality foundations and early assurance  |  Week 1
a. Learning outcome
1. Explain the role of quality assurance and navigate the tools used to investigate a web application.
b. What we teach
1. Client: Sends requests to a service
2. Server: Processes requests and returns results
3. Browser: Displays and runs the web interface
4. Operating system: Hosts the application tools
5. Files: Store source code and test evidence
6. Environment: Supplies the configuration for a test run
7. Team roles: Identify who builds, tests, and supports software
8. Quality attributes: Describe what makes software fit for use
9. Verification: Check work against specified requirements
10. Validation: Check whether the result meets user needs
11. Defect: Identify behavior that fails an agreed expectation
c. Practical work
1. Explore the existing website
2. Map its main user flows
3. Record three quality risks
4. Inspect one request in browser developer tools
d. Evidence of learning
1. Submit an environment checklist and a feature map.
2. Explain why a successful click alone is not proof that the correct outcome occurred.
Quality foundations and early assurance  |  Week 2
a. Learning outcome
1. Follow a feature from an idea to maintenance and improve its requirements before implementation.
b. What we teach
1. Planning: Establish the purpose and scope of a change
2. Requirements Analysis: Describe the behavior users need
3. Design: Define how the solution will work
4. Development (implementation): Build the agreed behavior
5. Testing: Evaluate the implementation against expectations
6. Deployment: Deliver the tested change
7. Maintenance: Support and improve the released system
8. Agile: Deliver and learn through short iterations
9. Sequential models: Organize work into ordered stages
10. Reviews: Find issues before implementation
11. Testability: Make expected behavior observable
12. Risk: Prioritize likely or costly failures
13. Acceptance criteria: State measurable completion conditions
14. Feedback: Revisit earlier decisions when evidence changes
c. Practical work
1. Choose a component on the existing site.
2. Write its user story and measurable acceptance criteria, identify missing decisions, and review them with a partner.
d. Evidence of learning
1. Submit the lifecycle worksheet and revised criteria.
2. Identify at least one defect that a requirements review could prevent.
Quality foundations and early assurance  |  Week 3
a. Learning outcome
1. Plan the testing needed for a change and make coverage traceable to its requirements.
b. What we teach
1. Requirement analysis: Identify what needs testing
2. Test planning: Define the approach and scope
3. Test design: Specify cases and expected results
4. Environment readiness: Confirm the system is ready for testing
5. Execution: Run cases and record results
6. Defect follow-up: Track failures through resolution
7. Test closure: Summarize outcomes and remaining risks
8. Entry criteria: Define when testing can begin
9. Exit criteria: Define when testing can finish
10. Estimation: Plan the effort required
11. Responsibilities: Assign ownership of testing work
12. Scrum events: Coordinate delivery and feedback
13. User stories: Describe needs from a user perspective
14. Definition of done: Agree on completion expectations
c. Practical work
1. Prepare a small test plan for the chosen site component and link each acceptance criterion to a test scenario.
2. Participate in a short planning and defect-triage exercise.
d. Evidence of learning
1. Submit a test plan and traceability matrix with scope, risks, environment, data, responsibilities, and completion criteria.
Manual testing and technical investigation  |  Week 4
a. Learning outcome
1. Select test cases deliberately and explain what each case is intended to reveal.
b. What we teach
1. Equivalence partitions: Group inputs with similar expected behavior
2. Boundary values: Test the edges of valid ranges
3. Decision tables: Cover combinations of conditions
4. State transitions: Test changes between system states
5. Exploratory charters: Guide focused investigation
6. Positive tests: Check valid use
7. Negative tests: Check invalid use
8. Test oracles: Establish how correctness is judged
9. Risk prioritization: Test the most significant risks first
10. Smoke tests: Check essential behavior quickly
11. Regression tests: Detect unintended changes
12. Integration tests: Check interactions between components
13. Acceptance tests: Check agreed user outcomes
c. Practical work
1. Design tests for a form, filter, or score rule.
2. Include empty input, valid and invalid values, boundaries, state changes, and recovery after an error.
d. Evidence of learning
1. Preconditions: State what must be true before the case
2. Test data: Record the inputs
3. Steps: Describe the actions
4. Expected results: Define the correct outcome
5. Rationale: Explain why the case matters
6. Demonstrate a decision table or state model instead of listing only happy paths.
Manual testing and technical investigation  |  Week 5
a. Learning outcome
1. Run a repeatable test session and produce evidence that another person can use.
b. What we teach
1. Execution records: Preserve the result of each run
2. Environment versions: Identify the exact system tested
3. Defect lifecycle: Follow an issue from discovery to closure
4. Severity: Describe the impact of a defect
5. Priority: Decide how urgently to address it
6. Reproduction steps: Make a failure repeatable
7. Screenshots: Capture visible evidence
8. Logs: Capture system evidence
9. Retesting: Verify a specific fix
10. Regression: Check for related breakage
11. Triage: Decide ownership and next action
12. Test summaries: Communicate the overall result
13. Release uncertainty: State what the evidence does not establish
c. Practical work
1. Execute the Module 4 suite in the test environment.
2. Investigate a seeded or naturally occurring failure and distinguish a product defect from bad data, environment failure, or an incorrect test.
d. Evidence of learning
1. Submit results and reproducible defect reports.
2. Expected behavior: State what should happen
3. Actual behavior: State what happened
4. Impact: Explain who or what is affected
5. Conditions: Identify the environment and inputs
6. Evidence: Attach material that supports the finding

sections.title: 13. Module 06 Web APIs and data basics

blocks.text: Manual testing and technical investigation  |  Week 6
a. Learning outcome
1. Connect what the browser displays to requests, responses, and stored data.
b. What we teach
1. HTML: Defines page structure
2. CSS: Controls presentation
3. DOM: Represents the page as a document tree
4. Selectors: Identify page elements
5. HTTP methods: Describe the requested operation
6. Status codes: Communicate response outcomes
7. JSON: Structures exchanged data
8. Cookies: Store browser-side values
9. Sessions: Maintain interaction state
10. Relational tables: Organize structured records
11. Primary keys: Identify records uniquely
12. Foreign keys: Relate records across tables
13. SELECT: Retrieve SQL records
14. Filtering: Restrict query results
15. Joins: Combine related records
16. Data validation: Check stored and displayed values
17. Document databases: Store document-shaped records
c. Practical work
1. Inspect a site interaction, read a JSON response, and query a synthetic SQL dataset.
2. Reconcile a displayed value with its source record or mocked response.
d. Evidence of learning
1. Submit a browser investigation and SQL worksheet.
2. Explain how a correct-looking page can still contain an integration or data defect.
Programming and browser automation  |  Weeks 7 and 8
a. Learning outcome
1. Write small readable programs and understand the code used in automation tests.
b. What we teach
1. Variables: Store values
2. Types: Describe the kind of value
3. Operators: Perform calculations and comparisons
4. Conditions: Choose a path based on a result
5. Loops: Repeat operations
6. Methods: Group reusable behavior
7. Strings: Represent text
8. Arrays: Store indexed values
9. Collections: Manage groups of objects
10. Classes: Define object structure and behavior
11. Objects: Represent instances of a class
12. Encapsulation: Control access to internal state
13. Inheritance: Reuse behavior through class relationships
14. Interfaces: Define a contract for behavior
15. Exceptions: Represent execution errors
16. File handling: Read and write test resources
17. Assertions: Compare actual and expected results
18. Unit tests: Check small pieces of behavior
c. Practical work
1. Build validators for quiz answers or form fields.
2. Predict the output of short code snippets, repair faults, and write unit tests for normal, boundary, and invalid inputs.
d. Evidence of learning
1. Submit small programs and passing unit tests with at least one explained failure.
2. Use code-based quizzes to assess understanding rather than memorized syntax alone.

sections.title: 15. Module 08 Git collaboration and build tools

blocks.text: Programming and browser automation  |  Week 9
a. Learning outcome
1. Share test code safely and reproduce a test run from documented instructions.
b. What we teach
1. Repositories: Store the project history
2. Commits: Record a coherent change
3. Branches: Isolate work in progress
4. Pull requests: Propose changes for review
5. Peer review: Evaluate another person's change
6. Conflicts: Reconcile overlapping edits
7. Ignore files: Exclude generated or local files
8. Dependencies: Track required libraries
9. Project structure: Organize code and resources
10. Maven: Build and run Java projects
11. Gradle: Compare another Java build option
c. Practical work
1. Create a branch for a test change
2. Request peer review
3. Resolve a planned conflict in the training repository
4. Run the suite with the chosen build command
d. Evidence of learning
1. Submit the reviewed change and setup instructions.
2. Another learner must be able to reproduce the run without copying the original machine configuration.
Programming and browser automation  |  Weeks 10 to 12
a. Learning outcome
1. Automate the existing website with stable locators, synchronization, and meaningful checks.
b. What we teach
1. Selenium: Automate browsers with Java WebDriver
2. JavaScript: Write browser-test logic
3. TypeScript: Add type checking to JavaScript
4. Playwright locators: Identify elements by stable properties
5. Playwright auto-waiting: Wait for supported readiness conditions
6. Playwright assertions: Check expected browser state
7. Cypress command chains: Sequence Cypress operations
8. Cypress retries: Recheck supported commands and assertions
9. Asynchronous behavior: Handle results that arrive later
10. Synchronization: Align the test with application readiness
11. Fixtures: Supply repeatable test resources
12. Network stubs: Control a simulated service response
13. Browser contexts: Isolate browser state
14. Failure evidence: Capture enough detail to diagnose a failed run
c. Practical work
1. Automate a form in all three tools, then test a dynamic component.
2. Compare Selenium explicit waits, Playwright auto-waiting and assertions, and Cypress command chaining and retry behavior.
d. Evidence of learning
1. Submit a passing and deliberately failing example in each tool.
2. Explain locator and synchronization choices and select one primary framework for the larger project.
Frameworks APIs and continuous integration  |  Weeks 13 and 14
a. Learning outcome
1. Refactor a small suite so changes are easier to diagnose and maintain.
b. What we teach
1. Page Object Model: Organize interactions around page components
2. Test intent: Separate expected behavior from interaction details
3. JUnit: Execute and report Java tests
4. TestNG: Compare another Java test runner
5. Fixtures: Provide shared test resources
6. Setup: Prepare each test
7. Teardown: Release resources after each test
8. Data-driven tests: Run a scenario with multiple inputs
9. Configuration: Separate environment settings from test logic
10. Reports: Present execution results
11. Test independence: Avoid dependence on execution order
12. Cleanup: Restore reusable test state
13. Naming: Make test purpose clear
14. Flakiness analysis: Investigate inconsistent results
15. Retries: Avoid concealing persistent failures
c. Practical work
1. Refactor the Module 9 tests, introduce synthetic test-data variants, and change one component to observe the cost of maintenance.
2. Run tests individually and as a suite.
d. Evidence of learning
1. Submit a documented framework and a before-and-after maintenance explanation.
2. Retries must not hide persistent failures; each failure needs evidence.

sections.title: 18. Module 11 Karate API and integration testing

blocks.text: Frameworks APIs and continuous integration  |  Weeks 15 and 16
a. Learning outcome
1. Validate service behavior and show agreement between the user interface and the underlying data.
b. What we teach
1. Karate feature files: Organize API scenarios
2. Given When Then: Express setup, action, and expected outcome
3. Requests: Define the service call
4. Headers: Supply request metadata
5. Authentication: Establish identity
6. Authorization: Check allowed operations
7. Response assertions: Check returned values
8. Schemas: Check response structure
9. Match: Compare Karate values and patterns
10. Reusable features: Share repeated scenario behavior
11. Data-driven scenarios: Apply multiple test inputs
12. Negative cases: Check invalid requests
13. Repeated requests: Evaluate repeat behavior
14. Error handling: Verify failure responses
15. Mocks: Replace unavailable services for a bounded test
c. Practical work
1. Use Karate to test a synthetic score or form-submission endpoint, then reconcile its response with the page.
2. If no suitable endpoint exists, use a documented mock behind an existing-site component.
d. Evidence of learning
1. Submit API cases and automated assertions for valid, invalid, and unavailable-service responses.
2. Record whether evidence came from a real endpoint or a mock.

sections.title: 19. Module 12 DevOps cloud and service workflows

blocks.text: Frameworks APIs and continuous integration  |  Weeks 17 to 19
a. Learning outcome
1. Run tests in a pipeline and use the results to support a release decision.
b. What we teach
1. DevOps: Coordinate development, testing, and operations
2. Jenkins checkout: Retrieve the intended source
3. Jenkins build: Produce the artifact
4. Jenkins tests: Execute the automated checks
5. Jenkins reports: Preserve run evidence
6. Failure gates: Stop progression after a failed check
7. Docker images: Package an application template
8. Docker containers: Run instances of an image
9. Kubernetes Pods: Host application containers
10. Kubernetes Deployments: Maintain the desired application state
11. Kubernetes Services: Provide stable access to Pods
12. AWS compute: Run workloads
13. AWS storage: Retain files and artifacts
14. AWS networking: Connect and isolate resources
15. AWS identity: Control resource access
16. AWS monitoring: Observe system behavior
17. ServiceNow ITSM: Test incident, problem, change, and request workflows
18. ServiceNow catalog: Validate request records and Record Producers
19. ServiceNow controls: Test SLAs, rules, notifications, and access
20. ServiceNow data: Validate assets and configuration relationships
21. ServiceNow cases: Test employee and customer service workflows
22. ServiceNow integrations: Verify mapping, synchronization, and failures
c. Practical work
1. Run UI and Karate tests in Jenkins
2. Launch a Docker test environment
3. Inspect a local Kubernetes deployment
4. Map the environment to basic AWS services
5. Complete the ServiceNow workflow and validation exercises in the detailed teaching sections
6. Attach test and rollback evidence
d. Evidence of learning
1. Pipeline definition: Submit the executable workflow
2. Successful run: Preserve passing execution evidence
3. Failed run: Show how a failure is handled
4. Release checklist: Record the readiness checks
5. A green build must be followed by checks of the actual intended artifact and target environment.
Nonfunctional quality and AI assistance  |  Week 20
a. Learning outcome
1. Identify quality problems that functional assertions alone may miss.
b. What we teach
1. Usability: Evaluate how easily people complete tasks
2. Responsive layout: Check behavior at different screen sizes
3. Keyboard navigation: Operate without a mouse
4. Labels: Identify controls clearly
5. Focus: Show and manage the active control
6. Browser coverage: Compare supported browsers
7. Visual comparison: Detect presentation differences
8. Performance baselines: Record expected response behavior
9. Reliability: Assess consistent operation
10. Security concepts: Recognize common protection boundaries
11. Accessibility checks: Combine automated scans with manual investigation
c. Practical work
1. Review an existing-site form using the keyboard and a narrow viewport, measure a small approved performance scenario, and investigate a visual or browser difference.
d. Evidence of learning
1. Submit prioritized findings with conditions, evidence, and suggested remedies.
2. Keep load and security exercises within the instructor-provided test environment.
Nonfunctional quality and AI assistance  |  Week 21
a. Learning outcome
1. Explain what AI assistance can and cannot establish about software quality.
b. What we teach
1. AI: Introduce systems that perform tasks associated with intelligence
2. Machine learning: Learn patterns from data
3. Generative AI: Produce new content from learned patterns
4. LLMs: Generate language from supplied context
5. Tokens: Represent units of model input and output
6. Training: Change learned model parameters
7. Inference: Generate a result using a trained model
8. Context: Supply information for the current response
9. Next-token generation: Produce language step by step
10. Grounding: Supply relevant reference material
11. Hallucinations: Identify plausible but unsupported output
12. Evaluation: Judge responses against defined expectations
13. Microsoft 365 Copilot: Assist with workplace documents
14. GitHub Copilot: Assist with software development
15. Approved access: Follow organizational tool and data rules
16. Model availability: Check what the selected product permits
c. Practical work
1. Use approved Copilot access to explain a requirement or generate candidate cases; use instructor-provided outputs if access is unavailable.
2. Compare the response with the source requirement and manually identify omissions or unsupported claims.
d. Evidence of learning
1. Prompt: Record the submitted instruction
2. Sanitized inputs: Preserve the non-sensitive context
3. Original output: Retain the unedited AI response
4. Corrected result: Show the verified revision
5. Explain why fluent text and runnable code are not proof of correctness.
Nonfunctional quality and AI assistance  |  Week 22
a. Learning outcome
1. Use AI to improve testing work while retaining human ownership of expected behavior and evidence.
b. What we teach
1. GitHub Copilot: Draft and explain code for review
2. Microsoft 365 Copilot: Support requirement and document work
3. Structured prompts: State the task and required output
4. Case generation: Propose tests from requirements
5. Boundary suggestions: Identify edge cases to review
6. Synthetic data: Generate nonproduction test inputs
7. Test-code drafts: Create code that must be executed and checked
8. Refactoring: Propose improvements to existing code
9. Log summaries: Condense failure information for review
10. Debugging support: Suggest explanations to verify
11. Source checks: Compare claims with trusted material
12. Reproducibility: Record enough context to repeat the work
c. Practical work
1. Apply AI assistance to one existing-site component.
2. Compare its suggested cases with a manually designed baseline, run any generated test code, and review the differences.
d. Evidence of learning
1. Submit an annotated comparison showing accepted, changed, and rejected suggestions.
2. Independently justify assertions and disclose which artifacts used AI assistance.
Machine learning AI evaluation and the final project  |  Week 23
a. Learning outcome
1. Interpret a basic model evaluation without confusing model performance with application correctness.
b. What we teach
1. Features: Represent model inputs
2. Labels: Represent expected target values
3. Supervised learning: Learn from labeled examples
4. Unsupervised learning: Find patterns without target labels
5. Classification: Predict a category
6. Regression: Predict a numeric value
7. Training split: Supply data for learning
8. Validation split: Support development decisions
9. Test split: Evaluate held-out examples
10. Leakage: Detect unintended access to evaluation information
11. Class imbalance: Recognize uneven category representation
12. Confusion matrix: Summarize classification outcomes
13. Precision: Assess the correctness of positive predictions
14. Recall: Assess how many actual positives were found
15. Error metrics: Quantify prediction errors
16. Drift: Observe changes in data or behavior
c. Practical work
1. Use a small synthetic dataset in a guided Python notebook or a prepared results worksheet.
2. Compare two model outputs and explain errors, class balance, and why test data must be held apart.
d. Evidence of learning
1. Submit an evaluation summary and error analysis.
2. Advanced mathematics and model training infrastructure are outside this curriculum.
Machine learning AI evaluation and the final project  |  Week 24
a. Learning outcome
1. Design an evaluation for variable AI output and distinguish it from ordinary deterministic assertions.
b. What we teach
1. Evaluation datasets: Collect representative test inputs
2. Reference answers: Provide expected response examples
3. Rubrics: Define response-quality criteria
4. Factuality: Check whether claims are supported
5. Grounding: Check the use of supplied sources
6. Invalid inputs: Test unsuitable requests
7. Prompt injection awareness: Recognize attempts to redirect the system
8. Privacy: Check handling of sensitive information
9. Repeated trials: Observe output variability
10. Regression evaluation: Compare behavior after changes
11. Latency: Measure response time
12. Fallbacks: Check behavior when the model is unavailable
13. Human review: Resolve judgments requiring interpretation
c. Practical work
1. Evaluate an optional quiz explanation or hint component on the existing site.
2. Use recorded responses or a mock if a live model is unavailable.
3. Include correct, unsupported, irrelevant, and unavailable-response cases.
d. Evidence of learning
1. Evaluation set: Submit the selected test inputs
2. Rubric: State the quality criteria
3. Results: Record observed outcomes
4. Failure analysis: Explain the unsuccessful cases
5. Fallback checks: Verify unavailable-service behavior
6. Record provider and configuration only when a live model is actually used; do not claim a mock tested the model.
Machine learning AI evaluation and the final project  |  Weeks 25 to 28
a. Learning outcome
1. Demonstrate the complete testing workflow on useful additions to the website we already have.
b. What we teach
1. Scope: Bound the website changes
2. Risks: Prioritize significant failures
3. Acceptance criteria: Define expected behavior
4. Incremental improvements: Add testable components to the existing site
5. Manual coverage: Investigate behavior directly
6. Automated coverage: Repeat selected checks with tools
7. Pipeline execution: Run the checks consistently
8. Defect correction: Repair and retest failures
9. Regression: Check existing behavior after changes
10. Release evidence: Support the release decision
11. Communication: Explain results and limitations
12. Handover: Provide the test package and operating notes
c. Practical work
1. Choose a bounded group of components with the instructor.
2. Add or refine them in the approved test environment, then apply the course test plan, automation framework, API checks, and relevant AI-assisted or AI-feature evaluation.
d. Evidence of learning
1. Submit the completed project package and demonstrate it live.
2. Failure: Explain one unsuccessful result
3. Improvement: Demonstrate one change made after review
4. Limitations: State what remains unresolved
5. Site ownership, existing features, and unrelated work are preserved.
1. All learners use Selenium, Playwright, and Cypress.
2. We teach Java first, then the JavaScript and TypeScript needed for browser tests, including functions, objects, modules, promises, and async and await.
3. Cypress command chains need their own execution model; students do not treat them as ordinary promises.
a. Selenium
Teaching focus
1. Java WebDriver: Control a browser through Selenium Java code
2. Explicit waits: Wait until a specified browser condition is satisfied
3. Page objects: Encapsulate interactions with a page or component
4. Browser lifecycle: Start and close the browser cleanly for a test
Required evidence
1. Form and dynamic component tests with failure evidence
b. Playwright
Teaching focus
1. TypeScript: Add type checking to JavaScript
2. Locators: Identify the element a test will interact with
3. Auto-waiting: Wait for supported readiness conditions before acting
4. Fixtures: Provide shared test resources
5. Contexts: Isolate browser state between tests
6. Network control: Observe or substitute service responses during a test
7. Traces: Record execution details for diagnosing a failure
Required evidence
1. The same form flow plus a trace of a failed assertion
a. Cypress
Teaching focus
1. JavaScript or TypeScript
2. Command chains: Sequence operations using the Cypress execution model
3. Retry behavior: Check what happens when an operation is repeated
4. Intercepts: Observe or stub network calls in a Cypress test
5. Fixtures: Provide shared test resources
Required evidence
1. The same form flow plus a stubbed response scenario
b. Karate
Teaching focus
1. Feature files: Organize Karate scenarios in readable test files
2. HTTP requests: Specify the operation sent to a service
3. Match assertions: Check expected values in a Karate response
4. Schemas: Check response structure
5. Data-driven tests: Run a scenario with multiple inputs
6. Reuse: Share common scenario steps across tests
Required evidence
1. Positive API checks: Verify valid service requests
2. Negative API checks: Verify invalid service requests
3. Authorization checks: Verify permissions for the requested operation

sections.title: 32. ServiceNow catalog requests and record producers

blocks.text: a. Concepts and validation
1. Service Catalog: Explain the self-service entry point for requesting available services.

5. RITM: Identify the requested item and verify its submitted values.
6. SCTASK: Verify the fulfillment task and its relationship to the requested item.
7. Approvals: Test approval and rejection paths against the configured requirements.
8. Fulfillment: Check task assignment and completion before request closure.
9. Alternative paths: Test cancellation, missing information, and fulfillment failure.
10. Record Producer: Explain a catalog form that creates a record in a target table.
11. Field mapping: Check that producer inputs populate the intended target record.
12. Order guides: Recognize their place among the catalog entry types listed in the source.

a. Time and workflow behavior

sections.title: 37. Large language models and workplace Copilot

blocks.text: a. What an LLM is and how it works
1. LLM: a model that learns language patterns from training data
2. Tokens: units used to represent text
3. Inference: generating tokens step by step from context
4. Training: changing learned model parameters
5. A prompt supplies context; it does not normally retrain the model
6. Context limits and variable outputs
7. Plausible language can still be incorrect
8. Grounding supplies relevant material
9. Retrieval adds selected source content to context
10. Grounding and retrieval do not guarantee accuracy
11. Verify claims, expected results, and code against trusted evidence
b. Copilot in organizations
1. Microsoft 365 Copilot: organizational documents and productivity applications
2. GitHub Copilot: software development and code assistance
3. Copilot products use models; Copilot is not one universal LLM
4. Features and model access depend on product, licensing, permissions, and organization settings
5. Use employer-approved accounts and tools
6. Check the context being shared
7. Follow organizational data rules
8. Do not assume one license provides every model or all company data
9. Record the product and visible model; mark hidden model details as unknown
a. A simple response flow
1. User task and permitted context
2. product prepares the request
3. model generates a response
4. product presents the result
5. tester verifies the result against requirements and evidence.
b. Hands on workplace exercise
1. Use Microsoft 365 Copilot to summarize a synthetic requirement or prepare a draft test outline.
2. Use GitHub Copilot to draft a small browser test or explain a failure.
3. Compare the result with manually written acceptance criteria, execute generated code, and correct unsupported assertions.
4. Use recorded instructor examples if a license is unavailable.
c. Learning evidence
1. Explain tokens, training, inference, context, grounding, and hallucinations in plain language.
2. Distinguish the Copilot product from the model it uses and describe why available models may vary.
3. Sanitized prompt: Record the instruction without sensitive information
4. Original output: Preserve the initial AI response
5. Verification: Explain how the result was checked
6. Corrected result: Present the supported revision
7. Explain one accepted and one rejected suggestion using independent evidence.
8. Terminology: LLM means large language model.
9. LMS means learning management system, a different concept used to administer courses and learning records.
10. The AI foundations topic here is LLMs.
11. Official references: Microsoft Copilot overview https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/copilot/microsoft-365-copilot-overview
12. GitHub Copilot overview https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/get-started/about-github-copilot

sections.title: 39. Improving the existing website for testing

blocks.text: 1. The existing website is the shared project.
2. We add or refine test components in small increments as the course advances.
3. The instructor confirms which site and test environment are used for a cohort; the curriculum does not depend on creating a replacement application.
a. Forms
What students add or refine
1. Required fields: Reject a submission when mandatory input is missing
2. Format rules: Check that input follows the expected pattern
3. Clear error and success messages: Explain the result of an attempted action
What students test
1. Valid and invalid inputs: Check accepted values and rejected values
2. Boundaries: Check values at the edges of a permitted range
3. Keyboard use: Complete the interaction without a mouse
4. Recovery: Continue successfully after an error
b. Choices and dates
What students add or refine
1. Dropdowns: Select one of the available options
2. Radio buttons: Choose one option from a group
3. Checkboxes: Select or clear independent options
4. Date constraints: Enforce the allowed date range
What students test
1. State changes: Check behavior after a selection changes
2. Combinations: Test interactions between selected options
3. Default values: Verify the initial selections
4. Invalid dates: Reject dates outside the allowed rules
a. Tables
What students add or refine
1. Search: Find records matching a query
2. Sorting: Arrange records in the requested order
3. Pagination: Navigate between groups of records
4. Filters: Limit results to matching records
5. Empty states: Explain when no records are available
What students test
1. Expected records: Verify that the correct items are returned
2. Ordering: Check the sequence of displayed records
3. Counts: Check reported totals against the data
4. Combinations: Test interactions between selected options
5. No results: Verify the response to an unmatched query
b. Dynamic feedback
What students add or refine
1. Loading indicators: Show that an operation is in progress
2. Delayed results: Handle responses that arrive later
3. Disabled actions: Prevent actions while their prerequisites are unmet
What students test
1. Wait conditions: Continue when the required state is reached
2. Repeated clicks: Check behavior when an action is requested again
3. Timeouts: Handle an operation that takes too long
4. Retry behavior: Check what happens when an operation is repeated
a. Browser interactions
What students add or refine
1. Dialogs: Handle an interactive prompt
2. Additional windows: Switch to the intended browser window
3. Safe upload examples: Practice with permitted synthetic files
What students test
1. Correct context: Act on the intended frame or window
2. Cancel paths: Check the result of abandoning an action
3. Allowed file rules: Validate permitted upload types and sizes
4. Cleanup: Restore reusable test state
b. Scores or submissions
What students add or refine
1. A synthetic submission flow with visible confirmation
What students test
1. Data consistency: Compare values across the page and service
2. Duplicate submission: Check that repeated submissions are handled correctly
3. API responses: Verify the service response to an action
4. Error paths: Check the behavior after a failed request
a. Accessibility
What students add or refine
1. Labels: Identify the purpose of each user interface control
2. Visible focus: Make the active control easy to identify
3. Readable errors: Explain validation problems clearly
4. Responsive layout: Adapt the interface to different screen sizes
What students test
1. Keyboard flow: Follow a usable sequence without a mouse
2. Focus order: Move between controls in a logical order
3. Contrast review: Check that content can be distinguished visually
4. Screen sizes: Review the interface at the selected viewport sizes

1. A bounded hint or explanation with recorded or live responses
What students test
1. Grounding: Check the use of supplied sources
2. Usefulness: Assess whether the response helps complete the task
3. Unavailable response: Check behavior when the AI service cannot answer
4. Safe fallback: Provide an appropriate alternative after failure
